narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the admissions model estimated a 51.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. This means that, at the margin, the risk of failing was considered slightly higher than the risk of passing.

The most important reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile of your school at the end of Year 3, while accepted applicants were typically around the sixth decile. That gap strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure and outweighed everything else.

Your other top factors actually helped you. Your LSAT score of 36 was only slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37, and in the model it pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was above the accepted average of 3.23 and also pushed toward passing. These were the second and third most influential factors, but they could not overcome the concern from your final-year class rank.

Neither gender nor race was used in the decision. Family income and full-time status also were not decisive.

Ask the admissions office whether you can appeal or have the file reviewed in more depth. If your final-year grades were affected by an illness, family issue, or other circumstance, document that clearly. Consider retaking the LSAT to strengthen your profile; even a few points could shift a future decision. Finally, if you reapply, demonstrate that you can perform at a higher level in rigorous coursework, since the key issue was your standing among your classmates.
